summary.text:
Torfaen's outturn is a clean read. The paper is one covering document with no separate appendix — all tables sit in the report itself and every one foots on its own arithmetic. Our PWLB file matches §3.1.1 to the pound and to the basis point: 13 loans, £67,910,899, weighted 3.5331%, against their £67,911k / 3.53% / 14.50-year row.

The interesting shape is the refinancing ladder. A single £10m PWLB loan matures on 30 October 2026 — about ten weeks after Council heard the report — at 4.39%. Behind it sit £10.35m of PWLB at a weighted 2.27% running off in the following twelve months, and £10m at 2.07% by early 2029. That is £30m of PWLB, 44.7% of the book, refinancing off very cheap rates against a curve where five-year certainty prints around 5.34% and one-year around 4.95% (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026). The stated strategy (§2.3) is to wait — 'the expectation that interest rates will ultimately reduce' — and §3.1.1 explains the £30m of LA temporary borrowing at 5.34% is bridging that wait. The wait is a positioned bet; the three loans coming off make it larger.

The balance-sheet identity is puzzling but not raised in the email. CFR £129,090k − external debt £123,437k − other long-term liabilities £5,653k = £0 on the identity, but §3.1.1 states 'under borrowed... by circa £8 million'. Neither treating LA temp as external nor as a bridge gets us to £8m. Documented in the note; not part of a first-contact email.

Two smaller items of record. The Key Messages box openly names a breached prudential indicator (interest rate exposure — §3.3.5, average variable-rate investments £18.722m vs £15m limit) which is transparent and unusual. And §3.2.3 lists three specific LA lending placements (£5m each to West Dunbartonshire at 4.25%, Blackpool at 4.20%, BCP at 4.66%) — Torfaen sits on both sides of a market where this year's rates have ranged 4.15% to 8.50%.

On the debt side, on our afternoon's DMO curve 11 of 13 loans price below par with an aggregate indicative discount of about £7.3m, driven by four long low-coupon loans (two at 2.07%, two at 4.85% running very long). Their §3.1.1 says premiums remain expensive; that was their year and their advisers' analysis, and ours is one afternoon in August 2026. Recorded and scoped.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Council on 21 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your Key Messages box calls out the breached interest-rate-exposure indicator openly, which is more transparent than most reports we read, and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A cross-check first, which is how we would prefer to start these. Our file holds 13 PWLB loans for Torfaen totalling £67,910,899 at a weighted 3.5331%, against your paragraph 3.1.1 row of £67,911k, 3.53% and a 14.50-year average life. To the pound on principal, and to the basis point on the weighted rate. Every table in the report also foots on its own arithmetic. That's the part that means anything else we say is grounded in what you've written.

We wrote because of the shape of what's next.

A single £10m PWLB loan matures on 30 October, about ten weeks from now, at a coupon of 4.39%. Behind it sit £10.35m of PWLB at a weighted 2.27% running off in the following twelve months, and a further £10m at 2.07% by early 2029. That's £30m of PWLB, a shade under half your book, refinancing off very cheap rates. On the current PWLB notice, 314/26 (14 August, PM fixing), certainty rates are 4.95% at one year, 5.06% at two, 5.34% at five and 5.83% at ten.

Your paragraph 2.3 says the strategy is to wait, on "the expectation that interest rates will ultimately reduce", and paragraph 3.1.1 records that the £30m of LA temporary borrowing at 5.34% is bridging that wait. The wait is a positioned bet, and those three loans coming off inside three years make it a larger one. Whether that changes when to reach for term money is your call and your advisers', not ours — we're just noting the shape.

The temporary borrowing itself is worth flagging. It added £1.348m to gross interest this year — second only to the £2.314m PWLB line — and the inter-authority market it sits in has been very wide. Of the councils we've read, we've seen rates paid anywhere from about 4.15% (Gloucestershire) to 8.50% (Cornwall, for four days), with Staffordshire's lending book growing to £152m across twenty-five councils and Liverpool raising £118m of two-to-four-year money from seventeen. You sit on the other side too, and your paragraph 3.2.3 lists it by name: £5m to West Dunbartonshire at 4.25%, £5m to Blackpool at 4.20% and £5m to BCP at 4.66%. Wide spreads and rising volumes at the same time is the pattern worth watching, and it's at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One smaller thing worth reading. Your book prices below par on today's DMO repayment curve — 11 of the 13 PWLB loans, aggregating to an indicative discount of about £7.3m, driven by four long low-coupon loans (two at 2.07%, two at 4.85%). Your paragraph 3.1.1 says premiums remain expensive and no rescheduling was undertaken; that was your year and your advisers' analysis across it, and ours is one afternoon in August. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Your book is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

And a standing item. The liability benchmark chart at paragraph 3.3.7 is going to be in front of everyone with CIPFA's updates to the Prudential and Treasury codes coming through. We hold an interactive version with live data at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark — useful if you want to explore how the gap between the loans CFR line and the existing debt line shifts under different rate paths.

On training, four fit Torfaen. PWLB repayment structures covers the maturity ladder ahead. Interest rate risk goes to your paragraph 2.3 assumption. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets covers both sides of the £30m temporary bridge. Liability benchmark walks through what your paragraph 3.3.7 shows. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you find any of it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26, Council, 21 July 2026 (also considered by Governance & Audit Committee, 2 July 2026).
